title: Binary Search
statement: You get an array of distinct integers sorted from small to large, and a target value. Return the index where the target sits, or -1 if it is not there. Your running time should grow with log n, not with n.

example.caption: Check the middle (3 at index 2), drop the left half, then check again. Target 9 is at index 4.

idea.sentence: Peek at the middle. That one comparison proves one whole half cannot hold the target, so throw that half away and repeat.

jargon.plain: Every value is bigger than the one before it. This is what makes a single peek so powerful.
How many times you can halve n before one item is left. A million items need about 20 halvings.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: a sorted array and a target, e.g. [-1,0,3,5,9,12] and 9

compare.bruteLabel: Check every item from the left
compare.optimalLabel: Halve the live range each time

rows.name: Linear scan
rows.note: Look at items one by one. It ignores the fact that the array is sorted.

rows.name: Binary search
rows.note: Each look removes half of what is left. Only l, r and m are stored.

fast.takeaway: Sorted order lets one comparison rule out half the array. Doubling n adds just one more step.

stages.title: Live range
stages.note: l and r mark the part of the array that could still hold the target. At first that is all of it.

stages.title: Look at the middle
stages.note: While the range is not empty, pick m in the middle, rounded down.

stages.title: Drop a half
stages.note: Too small means the target is right of m, so l = m + 1. Too big means left of m, so r = m - 1.

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: If nums[m] equals the target, return m. If l passes r, every index was ruled out, so return -1.

edges.title: One element, a hit
edges.why: l = r = 0, so the middle is the only cell. This is why the loop condition is l <= r and not l < r.

edges.title: Smaller than everything
edges.why: r keeps moving left until it reaches -1. The loop ends because l (0) is now greater than r.

edges.title: Bigger than everything
edges.why: l keeps moving right until it reaches 3, one past the last index. Never read nums[l] after the loop.

edges.title: Two elements, the right one
edges.why: The middle rounds down to 0. It is too small, so l becomes 1 and the next round finds it.

gotchas.text: (l + r) / 2 is a float in JS. For l = 3 and r = 4 you get 3.5, and nums[3.5] is undefined. Wrap it: l + Math.floor((r - l) / 2).
Integer division already rounds down, so l + (r-l)/2 is enough. Go's int is 64-bit, so (l+r)/2 would not overflow in practice, but writing l + (r-l)/2 is a free habit that is safe in every language.
An empty slice gives r = -1, so the loop never runs and you return -1. No special case and no panic.
Pick one loop style and keep all its parts. With while l <= r you must write l = m + 1 and r = m - 1. Mixing in r = m can loop forever.

recap.pattern: Binary search: halve the live range
recap.key: Compare the middle with the target. The comparison tells you which half to throw away. Repeat until found or the range is empty.
moves: While l <= r, take m = l + (r - l) / 2
Equal: return m. Too small: l = m + 1. Too big: r = m - 1
